# Does it last?

```{r}
#| include: false
source(here::here("chapters", "_setup.R"))
```

```{r}
#| eval: !expr '!has_data'
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat("*No results yet.*\n")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
#| eval: !expr has_data
pa <- results$per_assessment
later <- pa[-1, ]
gee <- results$gee
glmm <- results$glmm
```

The PI asked whether the effect lasts past the recovery room
(Chapter 1). The plan answers this from the estimate at each assessment,
read together with its confidence interval. There is no formal test across
assessments (D-002, D-003, D-013). A later assessment whose interval
included one would not show that the effect had worn off; it would show
only that the data could not rule out no effect at that time.

## The effect at each assessment

Each row is a separate unadjusted logistic regression in the patients
observed at that assessment, so each odds ratio is marginal (D-007).
Risk differences are licorice minus sugar water, in percentage points.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: !expr has_data
#| tbl-cap: "Any sore throat at rest at each assessment: licorice against sugar water."
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Assessment = pa$assessment,
    `Sugar water` = fmt_prop(pa$p_sugar, pa$n_sugar),
    Licorice = fmt_prop(pa$p_licorice, pa$n_licorice),
    `Risk difference (95% CI)` = fmt_rd_cell(pa$rd, pa$rd_lower, pa$rd_upper),
    `Odds ratio (95% CI)` = fmt_or_cell(pa$or, pa$lower, pa$upper),
    `p-value` = fmt_p(pa$p_value),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
)
```

`r if (has_data) sprintf("At ninety minutes the odds ratio is %s; at four hours it is %s; and on the first postoperative morning it is %s.", fmt_or(later[1, ]), fmt_or(later[2, ]), fmt_or(later[3, ])) else ""`
`r if (has_data) sprintf("Sore throat in the sugar-water arm stays common throughout, between %s and %s, and the risk difference on the first postoperative morning is %s.", fmt_pct(min(pa$p_sugar)), fmt_pct(max(pa$p_sugar)), fmt_rd(later[3, ])) else ""`
`r if (has_data) (if (all(pa$upper < 1)) "At every assessment, through to the first postoperative morning, the confidence interval for the odds ratio lies below one and the interval for the risk difference lies below zero. The data are consistent with a benefit that lasts beyond the recovery room." else "At least one assessment has a confidence interval that includes no effect; see the table for which effects remain plausible there.") else ""`
These are descriptive estimates at secondary time points, with no
adjustment for multiplicity (D-003).

## Common odds ratios across the four assessments

The two models below summarise all four assessments with one odds ratio.
Each assumes that the effect is the same at every assessment. Neither
answers whether the effect lasts; the table above does (D-014). They
estimate different things and should not be compared as if they were the
same quantity.

### Marginal (population-averaged): the GEE

A generalized estimating equation with treatment and assessment as terms,
an exchangeable working correlation within patient, and robust standard
errors (D-007). Its odds ratio is on the same population-averaged scale as
the table above.

`r if (has_data) sprintf("The common marginal odds ratio is %s (%s; %d patients, %d observations).", fmt_or(gee), fmt_p(gee$p_value), gee$n_patients, gee$n_obs) else ""`
`r if (has_data) sprintf("The estimated within-patient working correlation is %s: a patient's outcomes at different assessments are substantially correlated, which is why the assessments cannot be treated as independent.", fmt_num(gee$working_correlation, 2)) else ""`

### Conditional (patient-level): the mixed model

A logistic mixed model with the same terms and a random intercept for
patient, fitted by adaptive quadrature (D-008, D-020). Its odds ratio
compares the odds for the **same patient** under licorice and under sugar
water. It is a supporting estimate only, labeled conditional wherever it
appears.

`r if (has_data) sprintf("The common conditional (patient-level) odds ratio is %s (%s). The estimated standard deviation of the patient random intercept is %s on the log-odds scale.", fmt_or(glmm), fmt_p(glmm$p_value), fmt_num(glmm$sd_patient, 2)) else ""`

The conditional odds ratio is further from one than the marginal one.
That is expected whenever patients differ a lot in their underlying risk,
as the large random-intercept SD shows here. It does not mean the
treatment effect is larger. Odds ratios are non-collapsible, so averaging
patient-level effects over a population with very different baseline
risks pulls the population-averaged odds ratio toward one (D-008). The
question the PI asked is about patients as a population, and the marginal
estimates answer it.
